rv.q: The drama sometimes feels sleepy, despite that mystery, and despite the thrilling aesthetics of Joanna Scotcher’s set design
It’s also a necessary balance to the successes of YouTube channels, which can explain and illustrate deep science with extraordinary clarity these days.
Even so, it’s a testament to the power of the play that it grips regardless and, I think, can withstand a divided response.
Alex Kingston is simply superb as Margrethe, bringing a sardonic tone of reality to the men's endless debate.

The latest team to have a go at unravelling its mysteries is led by Richard Schiff, from the American political drama The West Wing, alongside the impressive young Irish actor Damien Molony and former ER and Doctor Who star Alex Kingston.
Scotcher’s set is gorgeously evocative of an afterlife dominated by science and time.
But to be fair, he was not the only actor to have momentary lapses in this notoriously tricksy and cerebral vehicle which requires absolute focus.
I am dazzled by Frayn's understanding of theoretical physics and the passion he brings to this tale of flawed geniuses.

But there’s simply no way of getting around the fact that the current cast, at least at present, doesn’t exert the rigour needed for this of all plays, Schiff in particular seeming to drift in and out of the action (and his lines), only to swoop in suddenly with rather bizarre vocal crescendos.
But everyone stumbles, too often for it to go unnoticed.
But I wasn’t exactly gripped by this meandering and rather lukewarm production.
The ideas and the moral conundrums here are, for the most part, completely absorbing.

It is a dense, unabashedly ideas-heavy play. It is often thrillingly clever, but its density can be tough for us and clearly tough on the cast – of the three actors it’s only Molony who seemed 100 percent on top of the text on press night, both in terms of not stumbling occasionally and also feeling entirely present in the character.
Whatever the reason, this performance didn’t quite land in the way I had expected, is as much a mystery as the reason Heisenberg came to Copenhagen.
Copenhagen is a complex and unusual play and this production does much to recreate its power and grip, though without perhaps quite reaching the required clarity regarding its subject matter.

cn.t: Frayn's intellectually demanding drama about physicists and the atomic bomb proves timely and rewarding, though its complexity occasionally alienates. Strong performances help navigate the dense material, even if full comprehension remains elusive.
